title: The five thieves
hookLine: lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride rob the house of the mind

cards: You walk into the kitchen in the morning, and something is off. A drawer is open. Your bag is on the wrong chair.
Your wallet is gone. Nobody smashed a window. The back door was simply unlocked, and someone quiet came in while you slept.
The worst part isn't the money. It's realizing they were in your house and you didn't notice. Good thieves don't announce themselves.

They slip in when you're tired or distracted, and take what matters most. The Granth uses exactly this picture, and it says there isn't one thief but five, and they aren't outside. They live in the house.

teach.b: Today's word is panj chor. Panj is five, the same panj that's in the name Punjab, the land of five rivers. Chor is a thief, a word still used across North India.
The five thieves. The Granth names them again and again. Kaam: lust, desire that grabs.
Krodh: anger. Lobh: greed, always wanting more. Moh: attachment, clinging to people and things as if they could never change.
And ahankaar: pride, the swollen I.
One hymn in Sorath puts it plainly: inside this body live five thieves, lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride, and they steal the nectar, while the self-willed person doesn't even notice.
The house is the body and the mind. The treasure is the nectar, the Name, the peace of the last two days. And the thieves don't break in.
They already live there. So the Granth doesn't mainly point at bad people out there. It points inward, at five movements every human being knows.
Some Sikh teachers add something fair: each of the five begins as a natural energy. Desire, anger at injustice, wanting enough, loving people, a healthy sense of self.
They become thieves when they take over the house and run it. So the first step isn't to fight them blindly.
It's to know them: their faces, their habits, which door they use.
A thief you've recognized is already half caught. Tomorrow, who guards the house.

how: Sikhs are commonly taught the five thieves, kaam, krodh, lobh, moh and ahankaar, as the main obstacles inside a person, to be overcome through remembering the Name, honest living and the company of the sangat.

o: five robbers from an old Punjabi tale
five sins that always bring punishment
five inner thieves, like greed and anger

games.q: the five thieves — tap the pairs.

s: in the Granth, the five thieves are bad people outside
they live inside the house: the body and the mind.
panj, five, is the same word as in Punjab
ahankaar, pride, is one of the five thieves
with lust, anger, greed and attachment.

games.q: you've realized five thieves live in the house of your mind. what does today's lesson say is the first step?
o: know them: their faces, their habits, their doors.
games.why: a thief you've recognized is already half caught. the Granth names them again and again so they can be known.

practice: Walk through your day so far like checking the rooms of a house: which of the five has been busiest, anger flaring, greed wanting more, attachment gripping, pride needing to be right, desire pulling at you?
Don't judge it; just name it softly, the way you'd name a visitor: ah, it's you. Let the naming be enough, and rest in your breath, the house quieter now.

wordCard.voice: Panj chor. The five thieves: lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride, living in the house of the mind and stealing its treasure.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: panj chor, the five thieves: kaam, krodh, lobh, moh, ahankaar.

carryVoice: Your line: know the thieves. Five of them, and every one has a face. That's day two hundred thirty-nine.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 600 (Sorath, Mahala 3: five thieves within the body)
